title: Off-ball gravity
lead: How tightly defenders stay with shooters off the ball, and how often rolls and cuts pull help, from the tracking.

blocks.text: Gravity is the defensive attention a player draws without the ball: a great shooter's defender cannot help, a hard roll pulls a second defender into the paint. This tab measures two kinds from the tracking: how tightly defenders stay with spot-up players compared with a typical player in the same spot (spot-up gravity), and how many extra defenders a roll or a cut pulls (run gravity).

items.label: Help pulled
items.sub: of runs drew a defender other than his own within 8 ft

blocks.text: Room off the ball depends on the defense's scheme, the score and the other nine players as much as on the player. Frames within a possession are not independent; counts of frames overstate the sample.

sections.title: How much room off-ball players get

blocks.text: Mean distance from an attacker without the ball to his nearest defender, by where he stands and how far he is from the ball. This is the 'expected' room each player is compared with.

blocks.unit: of the way to the ball

blocks.text: Shooter types use the season aggregates (league three-point percentage 35.1%; percentages shrunk with 100 attempts of prior weight). Across the 172 players with 100+ spot-up frames (perimeter, 15+ ft from the ball, not just after his own screen), spot-up gravity correlates -0.02 with three-point attempts per 100 possessions and 0.11 with shrunk three-point percentage.

As a group, high-volume shooters were guarded 0.40 ft tighter than a typical player in the same spot; players with some volume -0.25 ft and players who rarely shoot threes -0.24 ft. Player by player the measure is noisy: several bigs who rarely shoot top the list on 100-200 frames, probably because they stand on the perimeter just before screening or when trailing the play, when their defender stays close for reasons other than their shot. Negative values mean looser than typical.

sections.title: What this shows and does not

blocks.text: It shows how much room players get off the ball by spot and by player, and how often rolls and cuts pull help. In these ten games spot-up gravity lines up only weakly with season shooting (correlation -0.02 with volume, 0.11 with percentage), so it is not yet a clean shooting-threat measure. It does not separate the player from the defense's plan, and the 'expected' room ignores the defender's own role and the shot clock.

If this becomes the topic: model room off the ball on zone, distance to the ball and the ball holder's threat, with a player effect shrunk toward his archetype; then test whether higher-gravity lineups get better shots for others.
